rows.author: A013;
rows.title_short: Nomination Speech Of Rep. Belmonte ( F.)
rows.abstract:
In nominating Rep. Pantaleon D. Alvarez from the
First District of Davao del Norte to be the Speaker of the 17th Congress, Rep. Belmonte cited his personal and professional relationship with the former who was a Member of the 11th Congress and then the Secretary of Transportation and Communications under the administration of former President Gloria MacapagalArroyo. He stressed that the nation should grant the incoming Speaker the same overwhelming mandate it gave to President Rodrigo Duterte. He stressed that despite a rainbow coalition, the 17th Congress can pass
important measures because the Members´ sense of
nationalism will always prevail over their political and personal interests. He committed the Liberal Party´s support for the quest for change which, while not easy, could be achieved through consensus and compromise. He opined that Rep. Alvarez (P.) will ensure that Congress will work together with President Duterte to achieve the people´s aspirations and welfare. 
SOURCE: House Journal No.1,p.15)
rows.status: Pending First Reading (Filed last 2016-07-25)

rows.author: I090;
rows.abstract:
Upon motion of Rep. Fariñas, the Chair recognized Rep. H. Harry L. Roque Jr. from Kabayan
Party-List for his nomination speech for Rep. Danilo E. Suarez from the Third District of Quezon to be the Speaker of the 17th Congress. Rep. Roque cited Rep. Suarez´ humble beginnings which gave him keen insight and wisdom on the pulse of all classes of society, and also stressed the latter´s advocacies and leadership qualities. 
SOURCE: House Journal No.1,p.15)
rows.status: Pending First Reading (Filed last 2016-07-25)

rows.abstract:
Rep. Daza, a member of the Liberal Party for half
a century and its President for five challenging years, nominated Rep. Teddy Brawner Baguilat Jr. from the Lone District of Ifugao Province as Speaker of the House of Representatives. For the record, he took pride in emphasizing that this was the first time that a Member who belongs to the so-called cultural minority was nominated to the highest office of the Chamber. He thereafter recalled Rep. Baguilat´s political career
and enumerated his achievements as a Governor and
Representative of Ifugao Province. He underscored
that despite regionalism in the current political air, it is by sheer intent that he was nominating Rep. Baguilat because all the Members are first and foremost Filipinos, regardless of regional, religious and cultural background, and underscored his Party´s hopes and ideals for the nation. 
SOURCE: House Journal No.1,p.16)
rows.status: Pending First Reading (Filed last 2016-07-25)

rows.title_short: Nomination Speech Of Rep. Zamora ( R .)
rows.abstract:
Upon recognition by the Chair, Rep. Ronaldo B.
Zamora initially acknowledged the laborious process of plenary and committee works and pointed out that the 17th Congress would require a majority leader who is not adverse to change, is ready to sacrifice even his personal and family time if they need to bring about legislative consensus, has passion for public service,
has an established track record in the legislature and proven public administration skills, and who will not fear or develop second thoughts in helping stir Congress into possibly unchartered legislative waters. He said that he can only think of one name and that is Rep. Fariñas whose qualities include the following, among others: a bar topnotcher, at one time Laoag City´s and the country´s youngest mayor, governor of the Province of Ilocos Norte for more than a decade, a
multiple term Member of the House of Representatives, an expert in the impeachment
process, and most importantly, a public servant who turns to prayer and the rosary on a daily basis as a venue for reflection and divine guidance. Rep. Zamora thereafter nominated, with immense pride, great honor and complete confidence Rep. Rodolfo C. Fariñas as Majority Leader of the House.
SOURCE: House Journal No.1,p.22)
rows.status: Pending First Reading (Filed last 2016-07-25)

rows.title_short: Status Of The Election Of Minority Leader
rows.abstract:
Rep. Lagman initially said that both the trimedia
and the social media, as well as other interested
parties are puzzled why Rep. Teddy Brawner
Baguilat Jr. has not yet been officially recognized as the Minority Leader of the House. He stressed that the House cannot democratically function without a Minority Leader; the Committee on Rules cannot function with only the Majority represented; and the House Rules provide that the Minority Leader and five Deputy Minority Leaders shall be automatic members of said Committee.
He posed the argument that it was inevitable and
uncontestable that Rep. Baguilat is the new Minority Leader. Firstly, he argued that as the runner-up candidate for Speaker, by tradition and practice, Rep. Baguilat is automatically the Minority Leader having garnered more votes than the other losing candidate for the Speaker, Rep. Danilo E. Suarez. He said that the validity of the customary practice or tradition of the House to officially consider as Minority Leader the runner-up or the candidate garnering the second
highest number of votes, has never been questioned
and has been invariably adopted from one Congress
to another that it has acquired the character of law or binding rule on the Members of the House.
Secondly, Rep. Lagman ventured that Rep.
Suarez had disqualified himself from seeking the
position of Minority Leader because he voted for
Speaker Pantaleon D. Alvarez. This, as he quoted the remarks of Rep. Suarez in the previous session
wherein the latter said that he cannot vote for himself and that he was casting his vote for Speaker Alvarez. He averred that Rep. Suarez was not prohibited from voting for himself, as he cited a precedent in the 16th Congress when the two losing contenders for the speakership, Rep. Ronaldo B. Zamora and former Rep. Ferdinand Martin G. Romualdez, both voted for themselves. He argued that Rep. Suarez had effectively joined the Majority when he voted for Speaker Alvarez, as he cited Section 8, Rule II of the amended Provisional House Rules which provides that Members who vote for the winning candidate for
Speaker shall constitute the Majority. He added that the seven votes cast for the latter may even be eventually declared invalid. Rep. Lagman´s third argument was that Majority Leader Fariñas was in estoppel because when he recognized Reps. H. Harry L. Roque Jr. and Raul A. Daza to respectively nominate Reps. Suarez and Baguilat after Speaker Alvarez´ victory was a foregone conclusion, he was fully aware that there
were two contenders for the position of Minority
Leader. When Rep. Baguilat bested Rep. Suarez, he
stressed, it was clear and unmistakable that Rep.
Baguilat became the Minority Leader. Rep. Lagman´s final argument was that the 20 Members, except Speaker Alvarez, who abstained from voting were neither with the Majority nor the Minority and were considered as “independent Members” as provided for by the last paragraph of Section 8, Rule II. He pointed out that said Members could choose to join the Majority or Minority in
accordance with the prescribed procedure. He
opined that Rep. Fariñas´ position that those who
abstained were members of the Minority, violated the spirit and phraseology of the House Rules. Adverting to a precedent in the 16th Congress wherein Rep. Zamora (R.) was automatically recognized as Minority Leader when he garnered three more votes than former Rep. Romualdez in their losing bid for the speakership, Rep. Lagman said that the election for the Minority Leader will be an exercise in futility at present because Rep. Baguilat´s eight votes were more than Rep. Suarez´ seven votes. . . .
(Continuation)
He pointed out that the provision that the
Minority Leader shall be elected by the members of
the Minority, will only apply when there is no clearcut winner for the position of Minority Leader like when two or more contenders are tied with the same number of votes. He added that the Minority Leader had already been elected by the Members of the Minority when they cast their votes for the contenders for the speakership. Rep. Lagman concluded that Rep. Baguilat must perforce be recognized forthwith as the current Minority Leader and remarked that the procrastination to recognize him as such was utterly suspicious, if not downright anomalous. 
(SOURCE: House Journal No.2,pp.78-79)

rows.title_short: Reaction Re: Election Of Minority Based On House Rules
rows.abstract:
As he noted Rep. Erice´s desire to raise a parliamentary question, Rep. Fariñas first reacted to the exchange of debates between Reps. Daza and Atienza because his name was dragged therein, and opined that it was Rep. Daza who was making an alibi or palusot. Rep. Fariñas initially alluded to the previous day´s session when Rep. Atienza clearly wanted to rise and pose questions but was prevailed upon by the Majority Leader to allow the Body to finish first with the nominations for the Speaker of the House. He recalled that the only position that was aspired for was for the Speaker and not the Minority Leader, this as he emphasized that Reps. Suarez and Baguilat both ran for the speakership. Thereafter, Rep. Fariñas referred to Journal No. 1 of the previous day´s session wherein Rep. Atienza raised a parliamentary inquiry as to who would elect the Minority Leader of the House. This, as he noted that no Member had objected to the approval of said Journal earlier in the session. He also pointed out that during the previous session, after he had responded
to Rep. Atienza´s parliamentary inquiry by citing
Section 8 of the Provisional Rules of the House on
membership to the Majority and the Minority, as well as the election of their respective Majority and Minority Leaders, the Members had the opportunity to object to his opinion as the Majority Leader. As he emphasized that the position that was aspired for in the previous day´s session was the speakership of the House, he stressed that the Body did not pursue the election of the Minority Leader, and that Rep. Baguilat did not run therefor. He added that Reps. Baguilat and Suarez ran against Speaker Alvarez but lost.
Rep. Fariñas asked what subterfuge or palusot
was being done by the Majority. He stated that the
Members participated in the election of the Speaker, and that as provided by the Rules of the House, those who did not vote for the Speaker would constitute the Minority and would thereafter elect their Minority Leader. He added that the aforementioned 20 Members abstained from and did not participate in the voting process for the Speaker, and could have participated in the election of the Minority Leader had it been so mentioned. A law or regulation is not repealed by the nonobservance thereof, Rep. Fariñas underscored, as it can only be repealed by an express repeal. He said that under the Constitution, each House of Congress shall promulgate its own Rules that would become
part of the law of the land. He maintained that traditions, customs and usages would apply only in the absence of an applicable law. Subsequently, Rep. Fariñas referred to the stenographic transcripts of the previous day´s session,
and quoted the exchange of remarks between
Rep. Atienza and himself on the definition of Majority and Minority Members. He reiterated that any Member could have then objected to his opinion as Majority Leader; the issue of electing the Minority Leader was not taken up on the floor the previous day; and Rep. Baguiliat ran and lost for the speakership of the House. He asked whether it is democractic to claim that the Member who garnered the second highest number of vote, which in this case was eight, should be proclaimed as the Minority Leader. He thereafter underscored that while everybody is entitled to his own opinion, his opinion as the Majority Leader was supported by the Members, this as he noted that nobody supported Rep. Lagman´s opinion. With respect to the distribution of invitations to
the Members of the Minority regarding the election
of Minority Leader the following day, Rep. Fariñas
explained that as the Majority Leader and chairperson of the Committee on Rules, nothing happens in the Plenary Hall without his permission. He said that he merely honored the request of the Minority to have the invitations distributed. He asked whether Rep. Lagman was afraid of the conduct of an election for the Minority Leader. He added that as the Majority
respects the Minority, the latter should also
show its respect. Pursuing his point, he emphasized that those who did not vote for the Speaker would belong to the Minority, regardless of whether they voted for Rep. Suarez or Rep. Baguilat for the Speaker, and would now have to vote their own Minority Leader. He asked how the eight and seven votes plus the 20 abstentions
totaling 35 can have a leader who garnered
merely seven or eight votes. Thereafter, Rep. Fariñas cited the provisions of Section 8 of the House Rules one by one, particularly on the definition of Majority; election of Majority
Leader and Minority Leader, and Deputy Majority
and Minority Leaders; transfer of membership from
Majority to Minority, or vice versa; the definition of an independent Member; and Committee assignments and memberships. He maintained that a Member cannot be forced to vote for the Speaker, but the provision of the House Rules is very clear that a Member who does not vote for the winning Speaker will be part of the Minority, this as he stressed that the Journal of the House had already been approved by the Body. 
SOURCE: House Journal No.2,pp.84-86)

rows.abstract:
Recognized by the Chair, Rep. Lagman initially
stated that the SONA is a concrete articulation of a President´s assessment of the nation´s status, as well as his policy statements and proposed legislation. He noted that both were particularly present in the first SONA of the new President. He also pointed out that it is the President´s constitutional duty and as such, the SONA should be a well-prepared speech to be read by the President that should ideally be devoid of motherhood statements, and with a minimum of adlibs. Before proceeding with his counter-SONA which he said adheres to tradition and manifests the political opposition´s common alternative advocacy and differing views as well as the position of individual Minority Leaders, Rep. Lagman underscored the Minority´s qualified agreement with the following presidential
pronouncements, either in the SONA or as previously announced: 1) banning of labor contractualization commonly known as “Endo”, to avoid or evade a worker´s assuming permanent status; 2) uncompromising campaign to obliterate the drug menace by arresting and prosecuting drug lords and pushers, dismantle drug syndicates and rehabilitate drug users and dependents but which should be within the parameters of due process and rule of law; 3) prioritizing the construction
and development of railway systems in the country; 4) the liberation of impoverished individual
farmers from the burden of irrigation fees since this is long overdue; and 5) the call for the full implementation of the Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Law and its adequate funding support. Thereafter, Rep. Lagman proceeded to the Minority´s dissent on certain issues. First, he said that the proposed revival of the death
penalty as proposed under House Bill No. 1 is a retrogression and that the revival of capital punishment even for heinous crimes is an anachronism while execution by hanging is inordinately aggravating. He stated that death penalty should not be revived for the following reasons: 1) it is not a deterrent to the commission of heinous crimes as validated by worldwide empirical and scientific studies; 2) death penalty is antipoor because indigent and marginalized litigants could not afford the high cost of caliber and influential lawyers to secure their acquittal; 3) human justice is fallible; 4) rehabilitation and not retribution is the thrust of modern penology; and 5) only God can forfeit
life, among others. Rep. Lagman said that another retrogression is the lowering of the minimum age of criminal responsibility from the present 15 to nine years of age as proposed in House Bill No. 2. He pointed out that criminal responsibility is a grave burden which is generally limited to adult offenders and those above 18 years old. He said that since children lack adequate discretion
and discernment, they must not be saddled with
criminal culpability at a tender age of nine. That is why, he added, under Republic Act (R.A.) No. 9344 or the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006, a child 15 years of age or under at the time of the commission of the offense shall be exempt from criminal liability. Moreover, Rep. Lagman stated that under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child wherein the Philippines is a signatory, State parties are urged to undertake the “establishment of a minimum age below
which children shall be presumed not to have the capacity to infringe the penal law.” He likewise said that the subsequent United Nations Standard Rules for the Administration of Juvenile Justice or the “Beijing Rules”, provides that the beginning of that age of criminal responsibility for juveniles shall not be fixed at too low an age level bearing in mind the facts of emotional, mental and intellectual maturity. He maintained that the Philippine Action for Youth Offenders (PAYO) and Children´s Rights Network (CRN) which are both children´s rights advocates, jointly state that lowering the minimum age of criminal responsibility from 15 to nine years undermines
the best interest of the child and would not solve
the problem of children committing crimes, and would result in negative consequences for children and the public. Rep. Lagman said that the third dissenting issue is regarding the conversion of the Philippines´ form of government into federalism. He stressed that the country must not venture on a radical constitutional change without a solid prior study delving on the pros and cons of federalism in the light of the following
unique Philippine settings: 1) the country has 7,107 diverse islands; 2) it has mostly financially strapped local government units (LGUs); 3) it has centuries of experience under a unitary system; and 4) it has a relatively
small land area of 300,000 square kilometers.
Rep. Lagman mentioned that there is also a prior
need to sufficiently rebut certain arguments against federalism, including the contentions that federalism would heighten ethnic and regional rivalries destructive of national unity; exacerbate imbalances in the development of regional states; and create overlaps in jurisdictions as to where the responsibilities of the state governments end and where the responsibility of the national government begins. He stressed that Congress has the preliminary jurisdiction to debate on the merits and demerits of federalism and would decide as to the mode of constitutional change. Adverting to the statement of President Duterte in his SONA that “human rights cannot be used as a shield or an excuse to destroy the country,” Rep. Lagman stated that human rights have never been used to ruin a country and that the universality of human
rights prescribes that law enforcers respect and protect human and constitutional rights, more particularly the absolute right to life of suspected criminal offenders. As he cited the words of human rights advocate Jose W. Diokno, Rep. Lagman enjoined the Members to defend Section 11, Article II of the Constitution which mandates the State to value the dignity of every human person and to guarantee full respect for human
rights.
(SOURCE: House Journal No.3,pp.62-63)
